1.pericope_label: Better is the poor that walketh in his integrity, than he that is perverse in his lips, and is a fool. Also, that the soul be without knowledge, it is not good; and he that hasteth with his feet sinneth. The foolishness of man perverteth his way: and his heart fretteth against the LORD. Wealth maketh many friends; but the poor is separated from his neighbour
debates: Whether the first proverb contrasts poor with rich: Ellicott thinks a rich man likely meant on the strength of a parallel passage, while Keil and Delitzsch refuse to correct this proverb into conformity with that one and deny that the word for fool can carry the sense of a man who trusts in riches.

How the second verse should be rendered: Clarke prefers that to be without knowledge is not good for the soul, and reports versions giving that a man should know his own soul, while Gill adds a reading that makes the missing knowledge knowledge of the law.
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch argue from the accentuation that the poor man is not the one separated but that his friend separates himself, and that making the poor man the subject would lose the initiative of the desertion.
Henry notes that because conscience tells men they ought to relieve the poor, they are glad of the excuse that they did not see them.
Keil and Delitzsch say the man blames God rather than his own madness, which had turned grace into licence and cast to the winds the instruction lying in providences.

5.pericope_label: A false witness shall not be unpunished, and he that speaketh lies shall not escape. Many will intreat the favour of the prince: and every man is a friend to him that giveth gifts. All the brethren of the poor do hate him: how much more do his friends go far from him? he pursueth them with words, yet they are wanting to him
debates: Who pursues whom in the seventh verse: Wesley reads the poor man imploring his friends’ pity, while Henry reports a second sense in which they pursue him with words, excusing themselves by telling him he brought his poverty on himself.

How strong the word rendered hate is: Clarke argues it means only to show a lesser degree of love, so that the brothers neither hate nor love but disregard him, while Gill keeps the full sense of a man reckoned a reproach.
outliers: Ellicott states plainly that the first half of a verse appears to have dropped out at this point, and offers a sense only for what remains.
Henry traces perjury back to untruths allowed in jest, saying those who can swallow a false word debauch their consciences until a false oath will not choke them.
Keil and Delitzsch render the courting of the generous man as stroking his cheeks, and define him as one easily moved to open-handedness rather than merely as a prince.

8.pericope_label: He that getteth wisdom loveth his own soul: he that keepeth understanding shall find good. A false witness shall not be unpunished, and he that speaketh lies shall perish. Delight is not seemly for a fool; much less for a servant to have rule over princes. The discretion of a man deferreth his anger; and it is his glory to pass over a transgression
debates: How the eleventh verse should be pointed: Keil and Delitzsch report that several old versions vocalised the phrase to give long-suffering and that Jewish scholars have called that impossible, preferring the sense that discretion extends a man’s anger so that it is long in breaking out.
outliers: Ellicott and Gill both note that the word rendered wisdom is literally heart, so that what is meant engages the will and affections and not the intellect only.
Henry observes that the repeated warning against false witness has gained a word, moving from not escaping to perishing.

Henry allows delight to a man of business, to refresh him when fatigued, while denying it to a fool who lives idly and abuses his recreations, and calls a servant set over princes a beggar on horseback.
Clarke turns the clause on forbearance into an attack on duelling, and says whoever sends a challenge should hang for it, since he intends murder.
themes: Anger held back and let go

12.pericope_label: The king’s wrath is as the roaring of a lion; but his favour is as dew upon the grass. A foolish son is the calamity of his father: and the contentions of a wife are a continual dropping. House and riches are the inheritance of fathers: and a prudent wife is from the LORD. Slothfulness casteth into a deep sleep; and an idle soul shall suffer hunger
debates: Whom the proverb about the king is aimed at: Keil and Delitzsch say it states a fact so that the king may see himself in it, Henry turns it on kings and subjects alike, and Clarke reads it as a flat description of a sovereign who rules without law.

Whether the sleep is fallen into or inflicted: Ellicott prefers that slothfulness makes the sleep fall upon a man rather than casting him into it, and Keil and Delitzsch refuse a correction that would make the line mean slothfulness gives tasteless herbs to eat.
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch quote a proverb naming three things that make a house intolerable: rain trickling through, the contention of a wife, and bugs.
Henry says no man has a good wife by descent or entail, and that the wisest have been deceived both in and by a woman, so no man may credit his own choice for one.
Keil and Delitzsch defend the Hebrew literature against a scholar who thought the Greek rendering of the word for sloth was needed to expose coarse verses.

16.pericope_label: He that keepeth the commandment keepeth his own soul; but he that despiseth his ways shall die. He that hath pity upon the poor lendeth unto the LORD; and that which he hath given will he pay him again. Chasten thy son while there is hope, and let not thy soul spare for his crying
debates: Whose ways are despised: Ellicott takes them for the man’s own, which he will not examine, while Wesley glosses the phrase as the commands of God.

What the second line of the eighteenth verse forbids: Henry, Clarke and Wesley keep the received sense that a parent must not be disarmed by the child’s crying; Keil and Delitzsch make the soul the object and read it as a warning not to go so far as to kill him; and Ellicott offers both that and a third sense, not to let him perish for want of chastisement, without deciding.
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch keep the received text against a conjecture giving he that scattereth his ways, calling it foreign to the style of the book and superfluous.
Henry notes that the verb for lending means lending upon interest, and that the giver should take as much comfort in it as a moneylender who has placed a sum in good hands.
Henry reads the margin, which gives what a man has done rather than what he has given, and infers that the poor themselves may be charitable to one another.

19.pericope_label: A man of great wrath shall suffer punishment: for if thou deliver him, yet thou must do it again. Hear counsel, and receive instruction, that thou mayest be wise in thy latter end. There are many devices in a man’s heart; nevertheless the counsel of the LORD, that shall stand. The desire of a man is his kindness: and a poor man is better than a liar
debates: Who the man of great wrath is: Henry allows two readings, one of a passionate man whose friends must rescue him repeatedly, the other of the child of the previous verse crying out against the rod, and thinks them equally good.

What the twenty-second verse means: Keil and Delitzsch lay out four interpretations of the first line, examine a fifth, ask whether it is even true when stated so generally, and leave the question unsettled; Ellicott offers two senses without choosing.
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch report that the first word of the nineteenth verse yields no appropriate meaning in the written text, dismiss two Arabic derivations proposed for it, and add drily that tow rather than gravel would suit the word for wrath.
Keil and Delitzsch correct the rendering of the twentieth verse, arguing it means henceforth rather than at last, so that a man must break with the undisciplined beginning of his life.
Henry notes that God’s counsel often breaks men’s measures while their devices cannot alter his counsel or put him upon new ones.
themes: Passion that must be paid for

23.pericope_label: The fear of the LORD tendeth to life: and he that hath it shall abide satisfied; he shall not be visited with evil. A slothful man hideth his hand in his bosom, and will not so much as bring it to his mouth again. Smite a scorner, and the simple will beware: and reprove one that hath understanding, and he will understand knowledge. He that wasteth his father, and chaseth away his mother, is a son that causeth shame, and bringeth reproach
debates: Where the sluggard puts his hand: Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott prefer the dish set in the middle of an eastern table, noting that the bosom reading makes the saying a hyperbole, while Henry keeps the bosom and Gill canvasses three possibilities including a pot over the fire.

What the last verse says the son does to his mother: Clarke reports that the common Latin reading has him expelling her, while his old English Bible followed a copy that had him shunning her and leaving her to penury.
outliers: Ellicott marks a difference between the covenants, saying the later promise is not immunity from trouble, which may be needed for advance in holiness, but protection within it.
Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott both concede that punishment does the scorner himself no good, and that the smiting is for the sake of the simple who is watching.
Henry says that if correction does not cure the infected it may prevent the spreading of the infection.

27.pericope_label: Cease, my son, to hear the instruction that causeth to err from the words of knowledge. An ungodly witness scorneth judgment: and the mouth of the wicked devoureth iniquity. Judgments are prepared for scorners, and stripes for the back of fools
debates: What the twenty-seventh verse commands: Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott read it as irony, telling a man to stop learning if he means only to desert what he learns, while Henry and Gill take it straight, as a warning against teachers who draw the young from good principles.

Whose judgments are prepared for scorners: Keil and Delitzsch insist the word never means punishment inflicted by a court but always the judgments of God, while Henry and Clarke give the magistrate a share and Gill claims both.
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch refuse an emendation that would read justice for mischief and give, the mouth of the wicked murders that which is right, replying that the two verb forms interchange in the plain sense of swallowing.
Keil and Delitzsch distinguish providential chastisements visited by God in history from the strokes laid on a fool by one instructing him, and deny that a blow mentioned earlier belongs to either.
Henry describes the trade of the false instructor as teaching a young man how to palliate the sins he has a mind to and stop the mouth of his own conscience.
